papers.title: Statistical analysis plan for the feasibility trial assessing external trigeminal nerve stimulation versus sham stimulation for ADHD in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years (the eTNS4ADHD trial)
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: External trigeminal nerve stimulation (eTNS) is a non-invasive intervention being investigated as a potential treatment for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents. The eTNS4ADHD trial aims to assess the feasibility of conducting a larger randomised clinical trial comparing active eTNS with sham stimulation. This paper presents the prespecified statistical analysis plan for the trial. Methods: The eTNS4ADHD trial is a multicentre, parallel-group, randomised pilot and feasibility trial involving children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years with ADHD. Participants are allocated to four weeks of active eTNS or sham stimulation. Feasibility outcomes include recruitment, treatment compliance, acceptability, follow-up completion, and concomitant treatment use. Exploratory clinical outcomes include ADHD symptoms, school absence, emotional lability, functional impairment, quality of life, sleep quality, and adverse events. All analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. Feasibility outcomes will primarily be assessed using proportions with 95% confidence intervals, while exploratory clinical outcomes will be analysed using regression models or non-parametric methods, as appropriate. Two independent statisticians blinded to treatment allocation will conduct the analyses, and blinded conclusions will be prepared before unblinding. Discussion: This statistical analysis plan was finalised before unblinding to promote transparency and minimise the risk of selective analyses and reporting. Given the feasibility design and limited statistical power, exploratory clinical findings will be considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The results will inform the feasibility, outcome selection, sample size estimation, and statistical methodology of a future definitive randomised clinical trial evaluating eTNS for ADHD in children and adolescents. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06655610.

papers.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
papers.abstract: SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.

papers.title: Improved Sleep and Clinical Outcomes Following a Single-Session Intervention among Adolescents with Borderline Personality Disorder Features
papers.abstract: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious mental illness that often emerges in adolescence. Although efficacious treatments have been developed, they are often lengthy, expensive, inaccessible, and require specialized training to deliver. Optimizing BPD prevention and early treatment is an important public health priority. Disrupted sleep is closely linked to key BPD features, and prior research has documented a range of sleep problems among BPD samples that appear to worsen symptom course and duration. This intervention trial (NCT04507308) assessed the effects of a single-session sleep-focused treatment on adolescent sleep and BPD-related symptoms. Fifty-seven adolescents (ages 13-18) with 3+ clinically impairing BPD features and at least some self-reported sleep-related difficulties participated with a caregiver. Participants completed baseline surveys, interviews, and 10-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) protocol to examine BPD symptoms and sleep in daily life. Youth also collected at-home ambulatory electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings before undergoing the treatment informed by the Transdiagnostic Sleep and Circadian Intervention. Post-treatment, youth practiced their new sleep routine for approximately one month before undergoing reassessment (EMA, EEG, surveys). Many indices of sleep quantity and quality improved across both objective (EEG) and subjective assessments (EMA and self- and caregiver-report). Youth reported an earlier clock time at sleep onset and earlier waketime, more sleep, and fewer awakenings in daily life. Every sleep-related questionnaire score improved at post-intervention and was maintained at one-month follow-up. Multiple (though not all) indices of BPD symptoms also improved significantly. Findings suggest sleep may be a promising intervention target for at-risk youth.

papers.title: Wearable-derived daily steps and first recorded cardiovascular diagnoses: outpatient and acute care in All of Us
papers.abstract: Wearable-derived daily step counts are associated with cardiovascular health, but associations with the setting of cardiovascular disease (CVD) recording are less clear. We conducted a retrospective landmark cohort study using linked Fitbit, survey, and electronic health record data from the All of Us Research Program. Steps were averaged over the year before baseline. Eligibility required post-baseline sleep coverage and survey completeness, and classifiable pre-baseline smoking and drinking information; former smokers were excluded. After excluding participants with primary or secondary CVD recorded before baseline and 1,470 with either status during the first post-baseline year, outcomes were classified by the first qualifying primary CVD record during years two and three; a single qualifying outpatient record was sufficient. Among 8,292 participants, 5,780 had no recorded CVD, 2,127 had outpatient recording, and 385 had acute-care recording. Multinomial models adjusted for age, sex at birth, smoking, and drinking categories. Each one-standard-deviation increase in step count (3,299 steps/day) was associated with lower odds of outpatient recording versus no recorded CVD (odds ratio 0.786, 95% confidence interval 0.744-0.830), acute-care recording versus no recorded CVD (0.659, 0.586-0.742), and acute-care versus outpatient recording (0.839, 0.742-0.948). Both associations relative to no recorded CVD remained inverse across the tested hypothetical allocations of 455 missing-setting cases, whereas the acute-care-versus-outpatient point estimate approached or crossed the null under some scenarios. Secondary exploratory mediation analyses using a pooled score combining sleep, mental-health, and clinical-burden measures identified indirect associations for both settings versus no recorded CVD, but the between-setting indirect contrast was inconclusive. In this selected cohort, the findings highlight the importance of endpoint definition and recording completeness when interpreting wearable-EHR associations.

papers.title: "It Just Puts You Out!" Tranq Sleep, Sensory Discernment, and the Experience of Consuming Xylazine-Adulterated Fentanyl in Rural North Carolina
papers.abstract: Background: Xylazine, a veterinary sedative not approved for human use, has emerged as a consequential adulterant in the U.S. illicit fentanyl supply. Although a growing body of qualitative research has documented the experiences of fentanyl consumers exposed to tranq in large Northeastern cities, little is known about how xylazine is experienced in rural or Southern regions where the evolution of the illicit drug supply often lags behind its urban equivalents. This study examines how fentanyl consumers in west-central North Carolina detect, comprehend and respond to the widespread adulteration of fentanyl markets with xylazine. Methods: Between September and December of 2025, a seasoned interviewer conducted 25 in-depth, semi-structured qualitative interviews with fentanyl consumers recruited from both fixed and mobile syringe service programs in Gaston and Burke County, North Carolina. Interviews explored sensory discernment strategies, pharmacologic effects, and behavioral responses to the presence of xylazine. Data were analyzed using a combined deductive-inductive thematic approach in QSR NVivo 14.0. Results: Participants described a distinctive repertoire of sensory strategies for identifying xylazine in their fentanyl supply, including the appearance of drug residue on foil, bitterness and chemical odor when smoked, and altered viscosity when injected. A minority described an inability to detect xylazine through sensory cues. Participants consistently distinguished a profound involuntary sedation they called tranq sleep from the familiar opioid nod, characterizing it by nearly instantaneous loss of consciousness with severe withdrawal upon awakening. While nearly all participants expressed strong aversion to xylazine, a meaningful minority valued its amplifying effects to improve a diminishing fentanyl high. Conclusions: This study offers among the first qualitative description of xylazine exposure in a rural fentanyl market. Findings extend the xylazine literature geographically and pharmacologically and underscore the urgency of harm reduction responses tailored to the distinctive harms of xylazine. In particular, adverse health outcomes that accumulate during episodes of protracted and unarousable sedation, including physical injury, victimization, and the severe withdrawal syndrome that follows upon awakening.

papers.title: Objective sleep tracking for fatigue management in cargo pilots: six months of continuous smart-ring monitoring
papers.abstract: Aviation fatigue management estimates crew sleep from rosters and self-report. We examined how sleep duration changes around flights and with departure and landing times. In an observational cohort study, 13 cargo pilots wore an Ultrahuman smart ring for six months in 2026. We linked 1,504 sleep sessions to the flown schedule. Linear mixed-effects models compared each sleep session with the same pilot's rest nights, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Total sleep time was 48 min shorter on the night before a flight (95% CI 32 to 65 min) and 28 min shorter in the first sleep after one (95% CI 13 to 43 min). Later nights did not differ. Sleep duration varied with clock time. Compared with evening departures and landings, respectively, pilots slept 57 min less before a departure between 06:00h and 11:59h (95% CI 14 to 101 min) and 97 min less after a landing between 00:00h and 05:59h (95% CI 37 to 156 min). Flight direction and length showed no association. Differences between pilots explained 14.1% of the variance in total sleep time, more than six times the 2.2% explained by duty position. Fatigue risk management could plan rest around departure and landing times.

papers.title: Prototyping OSA: A New Framework for Predicting Cardiovascular Outcomes and CPAP Benefit
papers.abstract: Rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with major adverse cardiac events (MACE); continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) has not reduced MACE in randomized trials. We hypothesized that multi-domain machine learning would identify OSA subgroups differing in cardiovascular risk and CPAP response. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of SAVE trial data. After preprocessing, Gaussian mixture models were fitted; Bayesian information criterion and C-index selected five prototypes. Cox models estimated MACE risk by prototype. Baseline quality of life (EQoL), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), and Framingham Risk Score (FRS) were compared; an existing causal survival forest model estimated prototype-specific CPAP effects on cardiovascular risk. Measurements and Main Results: After preprocessing, five OSA prototypes were identified among 2,676 participants using 88 baseline variables. Prototypes differed in selected demographic, cardiometabolic, medication, and sleep variables, including smoking status, diabetes, prior myocardial infarction/stroke, antiplatelet/lipid-lowering therapy, BMI, oxygenation metrics, apnea-hypopnea index, and ESS (overall p<0.001). They also differed in baseline EQoL, FRS, MACE rate, and predicted CPAP response. Prototype 1 had the highest ESS, FRS, and MACE rate, whereas Prototype 5 had the lowest FRS and MACE rate. Using the causal survival forest model to assess prototype-specific CPAP effects on cardiovascular risk, Prototype 5 was predicted to benefit from CPAP (p<0.05), whereas Prototypes 1, 3, and 4 showed no benefit or possible harm. Conclusion: These findings demonstrate heterogeneity in cardiovascular risk and predicted CPAP response, potentially explaining neutral trial results. After external validation, these prototypes could guide trial enrichment and targeted CPAP use to improve cardiovascular outcomes.
